title: Lag BaOmer
hook: the thirty-third day breaks the mourning with bonfires, linked to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai

segments.voice: Yesterday, sefirah, the counting of the Omer, one quality a day. Your line was refine one quality. Did you take a breath before the test? Today, the thirty-third night of the count. Day six hundred eighty-five.

For weeks, the season has been quiet. In many communities, there have been no weddings, no live music, no haircuts. People look a little shaggy. Then, on one night in late spring, all over Israel, the sky fills with smoke. Kids have been collecting scrap wood for days: broken pallets, old doors, fruit crates. Bonfires burn in parks and empty lots. Families roast potatoes in the coals. In the north, at the foot of a mountain, huge crowds pour into a small town to sing and dance around a tomb. And the next morning, the barbers are busy, and wedding halls are full.
screen: `WEEKS WITHOUT WEDDINGS OR MUSIC.` → `BONFIRES ALL OVER THE COUNTRY.` → `A CROWD AT A TOMB.`

segments.voice: Lag BaOmer means the thirty-third of the Omer. Hebrew letters are also numbers: lamed is thirty, gimel is three, and together they're said lag. On this day, the mourning customs of the Omer season, which we'll explore tomorrow, are lifted. Why the thirty-third day? The honest answer is that the reasons came after the custom. One tradition from the Middle Ages says it was the day a plague among Rabbi Akiva's students stopped. A later tradition, from the mystics of Safed, says it's the anniversary of the death of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, one of Akiva's students. The Talmud tells a story about him. He criticized the Roman rulers, was sentenced to death, and hid with his son in a cave for twelve years. A carob tree and a spring of water appeared to keep them alive. They studied all day, buried in sand up to their necks to save their clothes. Tradition credits Rabbi Shimon with the Zohar, a foundational book of Kabbalah. Modern historians argue it was written much later, in medieval Spain; traditional readers keep the older attribution. Both views are held today. The mystics taught that on the day he died, Rabbi Shimon revealed his deepest secrets, and the house was filled with light. So the day of a death became a celebration, a hilula, a wedding-feast of a soul. And the bonfires are said to recall his light. His tomb is in Meron, in the Galilee, which is why the crowds go there. Children in some communities get their first haircut there, and play with bows and arrows. After weeks of quiet, Lag BaOmer is a break in the sadness.
screen: `LAMED-GIMEL: THIRTY-THREE.` · `REASONS CAME AFTER THE CUSTOM.` · `TWELVE YEARS IN A CAVE.` · `A DEATH DAY TURNED TO LIGHT.` · then, large: `A BREAK IN THE SADNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit by a fire or candle. If you can, light a candle now, safely, or sit by a fireplace, or just watch a flame on a screen. Let your eyes rest on it. Breathe. Think of a long stretch that's been heavy for you, or for someone close to you. You don't have to end it. Just let this one minute be a break in it: warmth, light, nothing to fix. The bell holds the time.
Lag BaOmer. The thirty-third day of the Omer: bonfires, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and a break in the season's mourning. Today's word.
Your line: a break in the sadness. Today, give someone who's going through a hard stretch one small bright moment: a call, a treat, a joke. Day six hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: On Lag BaOmer, the thirty-third day of the Omer, the season's mourning customs are lifted: weddings and haircuts resume, bonfires are lit, especially in Israel, and crowds make pilgrimage to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's tomb in Meron.

what a scholar hears: no Talmudic source for the day; a medieval tradition about the plague's end, and a Safed-era hilula for Rabbi Shimon, whose cave story is in Shabbat 33b.
